title: The Lighter Brief
overview: Busy Friday after the US midterms: the White House has a new chief of staff, and Mississippi's Senate race is still too close to call. Elsewhere, the Pope is back on the road after surgery, a Jamaican children's hospital turns 63, and people in 50 countries chipped in to buy a huge English estate for wildlife.

stories.headline: Stephen Miller Becomes Trump's New Chief of Staff
stories.summary: President Trump announced that longtime adviser Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, starting Monday. The change comes days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterms. Miller is best known as the architect of the administration's strict immigration policies, and Democratic leaders strongly criticized the pick. Wiles will stay on to work on political operations.
key_facts: Miller has been deputy chief of staff for policy since January 2025.
Wiles was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff; Axios sources said her exit was a mutual decision driven by the election results.
Democrats will hold majorities in both the House and Senate in 2027 and plan oversight investigations, including of Miller.
Separately, a federal judge paused construction of Trump's planned arch near the Lincoln Memorial for 14 days.
stories.why: The chief of staff shapes how the White House works with the incoming Democratic-led Congress on issues like immigration and cost of living.

stories.headline: Pope Leo Feels 'Fairly Good' as He Kicks Off a Big South America Trip
stories.summary: Less than a month after lung cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIV began a 12-day, three-country tour of South America, starting in Uruguay. He told reporters he's in 'fairly good shape' and encouraged people facing cancer not to be afraid and to get regular check-ups. Asked whether he's back to playing tennis, he said, 'Not yet, but I will.'
key_facts: Leo, 71, had part of his right lung removed on October 13 and was discharged October 17.
The trip includes 12 flights, 36 speeches and 10 cities, including high-altitude Cusco, Peru.
Uruguay, the first stop, is Latin America's most secular country; only about a third of people there identify as Catholic.
disputed: Vatican doctors say he is fit to travel and needs no further therapy, and medical care will be on board just in case.
stories.why: It's a cheerful recovery story with a useful reminder about the value of early detection.

stories.headline: Mississippi's Senate Race Is Still a Nail-Biter
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a little over 2,000 votes as of Friday afternoon, but nobody knows exactly how many ballots are left to count. Mississippi's 82 counties run their own elections and don't have to report to the state until next week, and the state has no recount provisions. A high number of provisional ballots has also drawn attention to how the state maintains its voter rolls.
key_facts: The Colom campaign estimated more than 15,000 provisional ballots; the state GOP chair estimated about 20,000 outstanding ballots.
The Secretary of State's office said over 9,000 provisional ballots had been processed by midday Friday.
Absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive until November 10.
disputed: The number of outstanding ballots is unknown; estimates come from the campaigns and parties, not official counts.
stories.why: The result could take a while, and the race is putting a spotlight on how elections are run and voter rolls are managed.

stories.headline: Charlotte's I-77 South Toll Lane Project Is Back On
stories.summary: The city revived the I-77 South toll lane project, and NCDOT has reopened its community engagement center for residents. Mayor Robert Harrington addressed the public pushback that originally led to the project's cancellation. For some longtime residents, it brings back memories of how the original I-77 changed their neighborhoods.
key_facts: The I-77 South Community Engagement Center has reopened.
The project had previously been canceled after public pushback.
stories.why: If you live or commute along I-77 South, the reopened center is a place to ask questions and share input.

stories.headline: Novant Health Paychecks Delayed by Tech Glitch
stories.summary: Thousands of Novant Health employees, including in the Charlotte area, found their direct deposits missing Friday. The health system blamed a tech issue with its new payroll distributor and apologized. It said pay should arrive by the end of the day.
key_facts: The delay was tied to a new payroll distributor.
Novant says it will reimburse employees for any problems the delay caused.
stories.why: Affected employees can ask Novant to cover costs like late fees caused by the delay.

stories.headline: Jamaica's Children's Hospital Celebrates 63 Years
stories.summary: Bustamante Hospital for Children in Kingston marked 63 years of caring for Jamaica's kids. It is the only specialist children's hospital in the English-speaking Caribbean, and its CEO thanked the doctors, nurses, teachers and staff who keep it running. It even has an on-site school so young patients can keep up with their studies.
key_facts: Founded in November 1963, soon after Jamaica's independence.
Treats children from birth to 12 years old across many specialties.
A new Parent Overnight Suite opened in 2026.
Some patients have passed their PEP exams while receiving treatment.
stories.why: A warm milestone for a place that has cared for generations of Caribbean children.

links.title: Bustamante Hospital for Children celebrates 63 years of service

stories.headline: Grenada Re-Elects Dickon Mitchell's Party in a Landslide
stories.summary: Provisional results show Prime Minister Dickon Mitchell's National Democratic Congress winning 14 of Grenada's 15 seats, securing a second straight term. The opposition New National Party, led by Emmalin Pierre, held on to one seat.
key_facts: The NDC got about 60.8% of the vote versus 37.1% for the NNP.
Turnout was 63.3%, with 60,151 ballots cast.
The NDC won the 2022 election by a narrower 9-6 margin.
stories.why: Grenadians gave the governing party a much bigger mandate than last time.

stories.headline: Novartis Confirms Tumor Reports in Some Zolgensma Patients
stories.summary: Novartis confirmed it has received nine reports of tumors in children treated with Zolgensma, its gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), since 2019. In two cases, there was evidence that the therapy's delivery vector integrated into patients' DNA, which could suggest a link. Patient groups are asking the company for clearer information so families aren't piecing things together from social media.
key_facts: More than 6,000 patients have been treated with Zolgensma.
9 tumor reports total; 2 showed vector DNA integration.
Both of those patients were treated and continue to be monitored.
disputed: Zolgensma is an FDA-approved therapy (since 2019), not experimental.
In most cases, no causal link between the therapy and the tumors has been established.
Tumor risk from vector integration is already listed in the prescribing information; regulators are reportedly reviewing the evidence.
It's not yet clear whether extra monitoring is recommended for past patients.
stories.why: Families of treated children may want to talk with their care team, and the findings could shape how the wider gene therapy field monitors safety.
